newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Indian prime minister nurtures roots in Pakistan.
newsitem.headline: Indian prime minister nurtures roots in Pakistan.

text.p: Fifty years ago Hindus slightly outnumbered Moslems in Jhelum, then a market town of 40,000 which traded salt and timber and served as a military outpost for the British, who took the area in 1849.
The Hindu community, in which the family of India's new Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral was prominent, left during the bloody upheaval of the sub-continent's 1947 partition.

Elderly Moslem townsfolk recall how Gujral's father, a lawyer who headed the Jhelum Bar Association and supported the Congress Party's struggle against British rule, organised the Hindu evacuation from this corner of present-day Pakistan.
"His father was the district chairman of the Congress Party and from his attitude no one could judge if he was a Hindu or a Moslem," said Younas Ali Shah, 87, a former city councillor.

"At partition, when many Hindu families had left, the remaining Hindu families from all over the area came to his house to board trucks for Amritsar. Avtar Narain (Gujral's father) was the last man to go," Shah remembered.
The Gujrals' modest two-storey home stands on the banks of the Jhelum river, 120 km (75 miles) southeast of Islamabad.

In its tree-shaded courtyard, 64-year-old Ehsanul Haq echoed the hopes of many Pakistanis who believe Gujral's links with his native land give him extra insight into the bitter India-Pakistan feud and an extra motive for seeking to end it.
"When he came here on his last trip, he said he wanted to have good relations with Pakistan and Pakistanis," said Haq. "Definitely he will do something if his parliament allows."
After partition many Hindu-owned houses in Jhelum were allotted to Moslem refugees from the Indian-controlled portion of the divided Himalayan state of Jammu and Kashmir.

These refugees, like most of the Hindus who fled Jhelum, have never returned to their homes -- victims of the Kashmir conflict that sparked two of Pakistan's three wars with India and remains the main source of acrimony between the two countries.

"We think our relations with India should improve and our conflicts should end so that both countries should prosper," said Qazi Hamid Mukhtar, a retired bank cashier. "We'll be happy if God gives them some sense that they should live in the same brotherly manner as we used to before the partition."
Gujral, a former academic with no strong political base, won the leadership of the disparate 15-party United Front coalition this month and took office as prime minister on April 21.
The government's survival hangs on the Congress Party, which had provoked a three-week political crisis by withdrawing support for the front's previous leader H.D. Deve Gowda.
Gujral, 77, who served as foreign minister under Deve Gowda, must tread warily to keep this apparently unstable set-up from collapse, but has made better ties with Pakistan a priority.
"When I look at the past few weeks gone by, I think India-Pakistan relationships have improved a great deal," he told Reuters in New Delhi on Saturday.
"Now, as prime minister, when I meet Mr Nawaz Sharif in Male, I will resume links, and I think we are moving towards discovering more and more areas of cooperation."
Gujral and Pakistani Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif were scheduled to hold their first face-to-face talks on Monday on the fringes of a regional summit in the Maldives capital.
India and Pakistan resumed official talks in March for the first time since a previous round broke down over Kashmir in 1994.
Gujral has promoted the idea that India is big enough to offer unilateral concessions to mend fences with its neighbours, but has ruled out any change in Indian sovereignty over Kashmir.
Pakistan wants Kashmiris to be allowed to vote on whether to join Hindu-majority India or Islamic Pakistan.

Gujral has many friends in the Pakistani city of Lahore, where he was educated at Hailey College of Commerce and Government College. They agree it is time to resolve half a century of rancour with India.

"The biggest problem is Kashmir," said Tahira Mazhar, whose late husband Mazhar Ali Khan and Gujral led the communist All-India Students Federation in the early 1940s. "We support them (Kashmiris), but we should not stop doing other things."
"Definitely it's a sign of hope," she said of Gujral's rise to power. "I think Pakistan should move forward...It's a time, a climate and we must make use of it."
Salima Hashmi, daughter of the late Urdu poet Faiz Ahmed Faiz, a friend and mentor of Gujral, said "his intelligence and familiarity with Pakistan" provided a sound starting point.

"I feel this year, not just symbolically, but practically, should be a year of growing up and acknowledging that there are differences, but also that human history has taught us that all sorts of issues can be resolved," she said.
